sections.title: Sentence Boundaries: Comma Splices, Run-ons and Fragments
sections.label: Introduction

paragraphs: A sentence needs a clear beginning and a clear end. When two complete sentences are joined with only a comma, the result is a comma splice. When they are joined with nothing at all, it is a run-on. And when a piece of a sentence is left standing alone with a full stop, it is a fragment.

These errors are less about individual words and more about structure: where one idea ends and the next begins. They are very common in timed writing, when ideas come quickly and the writer keeps adding to the same sentence. The good news is that there are only a few ways to fix them, and they are easy to learn.

blocks.title: The rule in one line
blocks.text: Two complete sentences cannot be joined by a comma alone. Every sentence needs a subject and a main verb.

paragraphs: Sentence boundary errors affect how easy your writing is to follow, and examiners count them as grammar errors. A comma splice in almost every paragraph makes even good ideas look disorganized.
On the positive side, fixing them often improves your grammatical range too, because the best fixes use linking words and complex sentences.
First, here are the three problems side by side. They all come from the same cause: not noticing where a complete sentence begins and ends.

rows: two sentences joined by a comma
part of a sentence standing alone

sections.title: Rule 1: Know what a complete sentence is
sections.label: Rule 1: Know what a complete sentence is

paragraphs: A complete sentence (also called an independent clause) has a subject and a main verb, and it makes sense on its own. Prices rose is complete. Because prices rose is not, because the word because makes the reader wait for more.
To find comma splices, look at each comma and ask: could the words on both sides stand alone as sentences? If yes, a comma by itself is not enough.

items.text: Prices rose. (complete)
Because prices rose. (not complete)
Because prices rose, people bought less.

sections.title: Rule 2: Four ways to fix a comma splice
sections.label: Rule 2: Four ways to fix a comma splice

paragraphs: Once you find a comma splice, you can repair it in one of four ways. All four are correct, so choose the one that shows the relationship between the ideas most clearly.
Using a linking word (the second and fourth options) is often the best choice in IELTS, because it shows the reader how the ideas connect.

rows: Prices rose, so people bought less.
Because prices rose, people bought less.

items.text: The city is crowded, many people move to the suburbs.
The city is crowded, so many people move to the suburbs.

sections.title: Rule 3: However and therefore cannot join sentences
sections.label: Rule 3: However and therefore cannot join sentences

paragraphs: Words such as however, therefore, moreover and as a result are not conjunctions. Putting a comma before them does not join two sentences, so the result is still a comma splice.
Use a full stop or a semicolon before them, and a comma after them.

items.text: Cars are useful, however they pollute the air.
Cars are useful. However, they pollute the air.
Cars are useful; however, they pollute the air.
Fuel prices rose, as a result fewer people drove.
Fuel prices rose. As a result, fewer people drove.

paragraphs: A run-on joins two complete sentences with no punctuation at all. It usually happens when you write quickly and forget to stop. Run-ons are hard to read, because the reader cannot see where one idea ends and the next begins.
Fix a run-on with the same four methods you use for comma splices.

items.text: Many students work part-time they have less time to study.
Many students work part-time, so they have less time to study.
Many students work part-time. They have less time to study.

sections.title: Rule 5: Fragments that start with because, which or when
sections.label: Rule 5: Fragments that start with because, which or when

paragraphs: A clause that starts with because, although, when, if or which cannot stand alone. It depends on another clause to complete its meaning. If you put a full stop before it, you create a fragment.
The fix is usually simple: join the fragment to the sentence before or after it.

items.text: Many people moved to the city. Because there were more jobs.
Many people moved to the city because there were more jobs.
The government built a new bridge. Which reduced traffic.
The government built a new bridge, which reduced traffic.

sections.title: Rule 6: Fragments with such as, for example and -ing
sections.label: Rule 6: Fragments with such as, for example and -ing

paragraphs: Another common fragment is a list of examples or an -ing phrase cut off from its sentence. Such as Kenya and Bangladesh has no subject or verb, so it cannot be a sentence by itself.
Join it to the sentence it belongs to, usually with a comma. For example can start a sentence, but only if a full sentence follows it.

items.text: Some countries have strict plastic laws. Such as Kenya and Bangladesh.
Some countries, such as Kenya and Bangladesh, have strict plastic laws.
For example, the UK.
For example, the UK has introduced a tax on sugary drinks.
Using public transport every day.
Using public transport every day saves money.

sections.title: Rule 7: Every sentence needs a main verb
sections.label: Rule 7: Every sentence needs a main verb

paragraphs: Sometimes a sentence looks long and complete but has no main verb, only an -ing form or a to-infinitive. The number of cars increasing every year is not a sentence, because increasing needs a helping verb (is).
Check that every sentence has a verb that shows tense, such as is, was, has, rose or plans.

items.text: The number of cars increasing every year.
The number of cars is increasing every year.
The government to build new roads next year.
The government plans to build new roads next year.

paragraphs: Two smaller comma habits make your sentences easier to read. First, when you join two complete sentences with and, but or so, put a comma before the linking word. Second, put a comma after an opening word or phrase such as However, In 2010 or As a result.
These commas are not always strictly required, but they make academic writing clearer and are expected in formal English.

items.text: The rent was high, so we moved.
In 2010, sales reached a peak.
However, the trend reversed after 2015.

paragraphs: Here is how good sentence boundaries look in real IELTS writing.

rows: Sales rose sharply, and profits doubled.
Coal use fell. In contrast, gas use rose.
Cities are crowded; however, they offer more jobs.
Because rents are high, many young people live with their parents.
Some countries, such as Japan, have aging populations.

paragraphs: These five errors are among the most common sentence boundary mistakes in IELTS essays.

rows: Prices rose, so people bought less.
Cars are useful, however they pollute.
Cars are useful. However, they pollute.
Many people moved. Because jobs were available.
Many people moved because jobs were available.
For example, Japan has an aging population.
The number of cars is increasing.

paragraphs: Use this routine on every comma and full stop in your final check.

steps: Look at every comma. Could both sides stand alone as sentences? If yes, fix it.
Look at every full stop. Does the next part start with because, which, such as or an -ing phrase? Join it.
Check that every sentence has a subject and a main verb.

cards.front: Prices rose sharply____ many families bought less food.
cards.why: Both parts are complete sentences, so a comma alone is not enough. Add a linking word such as so.

cards.front: Cars are useful____ however, they pollute the air.
cards.why: However cannot join two sentences after a comma. Use a semicolon (or a full stop) before it.

cards.front: Many people moved to the city ____ there were more jobs.
cards.why: Because there were more jobs cannot stand alone, so it must stay in the same sentence.

cards.front: Some countries____ such as Kenya, have strict plastic laws.
cards.why: Such as Kenya is not a sentence by itself, so it is joined with commas.

cards.front: The number of cars ____ increasing every year.
cards.why: Every sentence needs a main verb. Increasing needs the helping verb is.

cards.front: The bridge was finished in 2015____ reduced traffic in the city center.
cards.why: Which reduced traffic cannot stand alone, so it is joined with a comma.

cards.front: Fuel prices rose. ____, fewer people drove.
cards.why: As a result can start a new sentence. Because cannot, as it would create a fragment.

cards.front: Many students work part-time____ they have less time to study.
cards.why: Two complete sentences cannot be joined with nothing. Add a comma and a linking word.

cards.front: The government ____ to build a new hospital next year.
cards.why: Every sentence needs a main verb that shows tense. Planning alone is not enough.

cards.front: Smoking is harmful____ damages the lungs and heart.
cards.why: A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences. Because joins them correctly.
